common_name: Potter's Purple Butterfly Bush (Vigorous Reddish-Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Potter's Purple is a vigorous, large-flowered selection that benefits from an annual hard cutback in late winter to control its size and maximize bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving this vigorous cultivar plenty of room to reach its full size. Potter's Purple produces exceptionally long, densely packed conical flower spikes in a rich reddish-purple to violet-purple shade, each tiny floret marked with a contrasting orange-yellow eye, opening from midsummer into fall on gracefully arching branches clad in gray-green lance-shaped leaves. It is among the more vigorous and larger-growing of the older davidii cultivars, so give it room or plan on an annual hard cutback. Cut the shrub back hard to 12-18 inches in late winter each year, since flowers form only on the current season's growth, and deadhead through the season to keep new spikes coming and to limit self-sowing.

common_name: Lochinch Butterfly Bush (Silvery-Leaved Lavender-Blue Buddleja Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this hybrid tends to bloom on a mix of old and new wood, so prune more moderately than a typical davidii cultivar, removing only dead or crossing wood plus a light shaping cut in late winter.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun, where the felted silver-gray foliage colors best and the plant stays sturdy without staking. Lochinch is a hybrid between Buddleja davidii and the woollier, silver-leaved Buddleja fallowiana, combining soft lavender-blue flowers with a contrasting small orange eye and distinctly silvery-white, downy-textured stems and leaves that give the whole shrub a more refined, frosted look than a typical green-leaved davidii cultivar. Its slightly more compact, rounded habit and intensely fragrant, honey-scented flower spikes, produced from midsummer well into fall, have made it a long-time favorite of gardeners who want a butterfly bush with ornamental foliage as well as bloom. Prune more lightly than davidii types since it flowers on a combination of old and new wood, and remove spent spikes regularly to encourage continued flowering.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; this is a large, vigorous older cultivar, so allow ample room or plan on cutting it back hard each late winter to keep it in bounds.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, allowing generous room for this large, arching older cultivar to reach its full size. Fascination is one of the longer-established Buddleja davidii selections, valued for its big, gracefully arching panicles in a soft orchid-pink to lilac-purple shade and its strong, sweet fragrance that carries well through the garden. Its size and vigor set it apart from the many compact modern davidii cultivars, making it better suited to larger borders, screens, or naturalized plantings than to small foundation beds. Cut the shrub back hard to 12-18 inches in late winter each year, since flowers form on new wood, and deadhead spent spikes through summer to prolong bloom and reduce self-seeding.

planting.note: Plant divisions or small pots in spring in bright, indirect light to partial shade in consistently moist, well-drained soil; Aurea colors best with some morning sun but scorches in hot, direct afternoon exposure. In zone 9a, it may die back in a hard freeze but resprouts from the crown in spring; in zone 9b-10 it stays evergreen. Well suited to shaded rock gardens, terrarium accents, and mixed containers where its chartreuse color contrasts with darker foliage.

directions: Plant in bright, filtered light to partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, and shield from hot midday sun, which fades and can scorch the gold foliage. Aurea is a golden-leaved sport of the species, forming the same dense, mossy carpet of thread-like, rooting stems and tiny round leaves as plain baby tears, but colored a glowing chartreuse-to-gold rather than green, an effect that intensifies with a bit of morning sun and softens toward lime-green in deeper shade. Growth is slightly slower and less vigorous than the green species, making it easier to keep in bounds in a mixed shaded bed, terrarium, or hanging container. Keep soil evenly moist at all times, since Aurea browns and thins out just as quickly as the species if it is allowed to dry out.

planting.note: Plant divisions or small pots in spring in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained soil; Variegata is slower and less aggressive than the plain green species, so it rarely becomes invasive. In zone 9a, it may be killed back by hard frost but resprouts from the roots in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is evergreen. Grow in shaded terrariums, between shaded stepping stones, or as a small-scale accent groundcover in containers.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, since dry soil quickly browns and kills the thin, delicate stems. Variegata is a cream-and-white variegated sport of baby tears, its minute round leaves marbled and edged in silvery white over pale green, giving established mats a frosted, shimmery look rather than the solid emerald carpet of the species. It spreads by the same thread-like, node-rooting stems as the species but more slowly and with less vigor, which makes it a better choice for small terrarium plantings or contained pots than for open garden beds where the plain green form would be used. Trim back any stems that revert to solid green promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will gradually overtake the variegated portions of the mat if left unchecked.
